AI.result: Successfully solved four-dimensional linear equation systems across different fields; the modulo 2 VQLS is inherently singularity-free and adaptable to stabilizer coding theory.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the practical potential of VQLS in quantum computing, providing experimental foundation and methodological guidance for real-world applications.

title: Syndrome-as-Header: A Quantum Label-Switching Architecture via Uncorrectable Error Injection
summary: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that can tolerate control-plane timing uncertainty. Existing optical-burst switching (OBS) and quantum-wrapper-based packet switching (QW) rely on external classical headers whose jitter-prone processing must remain aligned with in-flight quantum payloads, creating guard-window or fiber-delay-line budget failures. This paper proposes Syndrome-as-Header (SAH), a quantum label-switching architecture that embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of an encoded payload. The proposed scheme uses Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes and builds a syndrome-space header codebook whose decoding regions remain distinguishable under correctable channel-induced syndrome deviations. Core routers extract the syndrome header, suppress the correctable residual channel-error component, and swap labels without measuring or decoding the logical payload. SAH supports FAST forwarding and VERIFICATION mode, the latter providing end-to-end consistency checking while retaining swappable labels. In NSFNet timing benchmarks with common per-hop quantum error correction (QEC), SAH eliminates the external-header/payload alignment condition, so timing uncertainty appears as memory residence and delivered latency rather than alignment-budget drops. With a $T_2$-based memory-residence penalty, the advantage depends on router memory coherence; for sufficiently long coherence, SAH maintains higher acceptance and throughput than OBS+QEC and QW+QEC under high jitter.

AI.tldr: Syndrome-as-Header (SAH) is a quantum label-switching architecture that embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of encoded quantum payloads, eliminating the need for alignment between external classical headers and in-flight quantum data, thereby improving tolerance to control-plane timing uncertainty in quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that can tolerate control-plane timing uncertainty. Existing approaches (OBS, QW) rely on external classical headers whose jitter-prone processing must remain aligned with in-flight quantum payloads, causing guard-window or fiber-delay-line budget failures.
AI.method: SAH embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of an encoded payload using Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes, building a syndrome-space header codebook with distinguishable decoding regions. Core routers extract the syndrome header, suppress correctable channel-error components, and swap labels without measuring or decoding the logical payload. SAH supports FAST forwarding and VERIFICATION modes.
AI.result: In NSFNet timing benchmarks with per-hop QEC, SAH eliminates external-header/payload alignment conditions, converting timing uncertainty into memory residence and delivered latency rather than alignment-budget drops. Under high jitter with sufficiently long T₂-based memory coherence, SAH maintains higher acceptance and throughput than OBS+QEC and QW+QEC.
AI.conclusion: SAH provides a robust quantum label-switching framework that eliminates alignment constraints between classical headers and quantum payloads, offering improved tolerance to timing jitter and better scalability for quantum networks beyond point-to-point links.

title: Geometric Mode Steering of the Quantum Mpemba Effect
summary: The slowest Liouvillian mode often bottlenecks the relaxation of an open quantum system to its steady state. Standard strategies circumvent this bottleneck by selecting special initial states or engineering the dissipator. Here we show that neither is necessary. We introduce a pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol that reshapes any given pure or mixed state before relaxation begins -- coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements -- at fixed Lindblad generator. By steering the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths, the protocol suppresses its overlap with the slowest Liouvillian modes. The prepared state then starts farther from equilibrium yet relaxes faster, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect, whenever two computable conditions hold: reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity. Our framework treats real and complex spectral gaps uniformly, and we demonstrate robust Mpemba acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems using operations available in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.

AI.tldr: A pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol using coherent rotations and nonselective projective measurements accelerates relaxation to steady state by suppressing overlap with slow Liouvillian modes, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect without needing special initial states or engineered dissipation.
AI.motivation: The slowest Liouvillian mode bottlenecks open quantum system relaxation; existing strategies require special initial states or engineered dissipation, and the authors aim to circumvent this without such requirements.
AI.method: Pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol: coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements reshape the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths before relaxation begins, at fixed Lindblad generator.
AI.result: The protocol suppresses overlap with slowest Liouvillian modes, achieving faster relaxation from a state farther from equilibrium (quantum Mpemba effect) when two conditions hold: reduced slow-mode overlap and larger initial distance to stationarity. Demonstrated in driven qubit and multiqubit systems using trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Mpemba effect can be realized without special initial state preparation or engineered dissipation, via a practical geometric steering protocol applicable to real and complex spectral gaps uniformly.

title: Structure-Aware Variational State Preparation for Quantum Basket Option Pricing
summary: Basket option pricing often relies on Monte Carlo estimation, for which quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) provides a quadratic speed-up. However, the practical benefit of QAE can be limited by the depth of the state-preparation circuit. We propose a structure-aware quantum state-preparation framework for QAE-based basket option pricing. The framework uses tensor-train (TT) rank information to design shallow variational state-preparation circuits. In the independent regime, TT ranks remove unnecessary entangling links from a hardware-efficient ansatz. In correlated basket settings, we instead prepare asset-wise marginals locally and train a compact latent block to match the basket cumulative distribution function. The Basket-CDF objective targets the basket pushforward distribution rather than the full joint state, directly aligning state preparation with basket-dependent payoffs. Numerical experiments show that the proposed circuits replace the exponential state-preparation depth scaling of exact amplitude loading with linear scaling, while maintaining low-percent basket-pricing errors. Additional sampling-based training experiments and an end-to-end QAE integration study support compatibility with sample-estimated training and standard QAE-based pricing workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a structure-aware quantum state-preparation framework for QAE-based basket option pricing that uses tensor-train rank information to design shallow variational circuits, replacing exponential depth scaling with linear scaling while maintaining low pricing errors.
AI.motivation: Basket option pricing relies on Monte Carlo estimation, and while QAE provides quadratic speed-up, its practical benefit is limited by the depth of state-preparation circuits.
AI.method: The framework uses tensor-train (TT) rank information to design shallow variational state-preparation circuits. For independent baskets, TT ranks remove unnecessary entangling links from hardware-efficient ansatz. For correlated baskets, it prepares asset-wise marginals locally and trains a compact latent block to match the basket cumulative distribution function (Basket-CDF objective).
AI.result: The proposed circuits replace exponential state-preparation depth scaling with linear scaling while maintaining low-percent basket-pricing errors. Sampling-based training experiments and end-to-end QAE integration study show compatibility with sample-estimated training and standard QAE-based pricing workflows.
AI.conclusion: The structure-aware quantum state-preparation framework successfully reduces circuit depth from exponential to linear scaling for basket option pricing, demonstrating practical viability through numerical experiments and QAE integration.

title: No Finite NPA Level Characterizes the Complete Quantum Set in the Simplest Bell Scenario
comment: Submitted to Physical Review Letters on 14 July 2026. Closely overlapping preprints arXiv:2607.13762 and arXiv:2607.13774 appeared on 15 July 2026. This work was completed independently beforehand and gives a distinct fully analytical proof with broader behavior-set consequences
summary: The Navascués--Pironio--Acín (NPA) hierarchy gives the standard semidefinite outer approximations to quantum behaviors. Whether \emph{any} finite level can already equal the quantum set has remained open even in the bipartite scenario with two binary measurements per party. We demonstrate that \emph{no finite level} is exact. For the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional $h_α=A_0B_0+A_0B_1+A_1B_0-A_1B_1+α(A_0+B_0)$, set $T=1-α$. Its quantum maximum satisfies $[ω_{\rm Q}(1-T)-(4-2T)]/T^3\to4/3$, whereas every fixed NPA level satisfies $[ω_L(1-T)-ω_{\rm Q}(1-T)]/T^3\to+\infty$. Under the corresponding boundary rescaling, an explicit expectation of the positive operator $ω_{\rm Q}(1-t^2)I-H_t$ converges to the Motzkin polynomial. A bounded fixed-level error would therefore make the Motzkin polynomial plus a nonnegative constant a sum of squares, which is impossible. Consequently, every standard NPA relaxation based on a fixed finite list of words in the measurement projectors strictly contains the complete quantum set, and its nonquantum behaviors accumulate at a local deterministic behavior. Thus, the finite-level exactness of CHSH and all one-sided tilted CHSH maxima does not extend to an exact finite-level description of the complete quantum set in the minimal scenario.

AI.tldr: No finite level of the NPA hierarchy exactly captures the full quantum set, even in the minimal bipartite scenario with two binary measurements per party. This is proven by analyzing the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional, showing that fixed-level approximations have errors that diverge in a specific scaling limit, which would otherwise force the Motzkin polynomial to be a sum of squares—an impossibility.
AI.motivation: The NPA hierarchy provides standard semidefinite outer approximations to quantum behaviors, but whether any finite level already equals the quantum set has remained open, even in the simplest bipartite scenario with two binary measurements per party.
AI.method: The authors analyze the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional $h_α = A_0B_0 + A_0B_1 + A_1B_0 - A_1B_1 + α(A_0+B_0)$, setting $T=1-α$. They study the scaling behavior of its quantum maximum $ω_Q$ versus fixed NPA level maxima $ω_L$ as $T→0$, and examine the expectation of $ω_Q(1-t^2)I - H_t$ under boundary rescaling, connecting to the Motzkin polynomial.
AI.result: The quantum maximum satisfies $[ω_Q(1-T)-(4-2T)]/T^3 → 4/3$, whereas every fixed NPA level satisfies $[ω_L(1-T)-ω_Q(1-T)]/T^3 → +∞$. Under boundary rescaling, the expectation converges to the Motzkin polynomial; bounded fixed-level error would force the Motzkin polynomial plus a nonnegative constant to be a sum of squares, which is impossible. Hence, every standard NPA relaxation strictly contains the quantum set, with nonquantum behaviors accumulating at a local deterministic point.
AI.conclusion: No finite level of the NPA hierarchy is exact for the complete quantum set even in the minimal scenario. The finite-level exactness of CHSH and one-sided tilted CHSH does not extend to an exact finite-level description of the full quantum set.

title: Exact No Signaling in Time without Temporal Classicality
summary: No signaling in time (NSIT) has often been treated as the clean operational remnant of noninvasive measurability. If an earlier measurement leaves every later marginal unchanged, the temporal process appears classical. We show that this inference is false. We introduce common fixed points (CFPs) of nonselective measurement channels as an exact mechanism that erases all marginal evidence of invasiveness while preserving disturbed outcome conditioned branches. For a qutrit ring subject to a local degenerate Luders measurement, we solve the full CFP manifold analytically. Every state on this manifold satisfies exact pairwise NSIT, yet every nontrivial member violates a Leggett Garg inequality, including the maximally mixed state. The violation is governed by finite branch displacement, not by residual signaling. Hidden variable reconstruction, entropic witnesses, protocol landscape scans, noise robustness, and finite shot simulations show that exact NSIT certifies only the disappearance of marginal signals after outcome erasure, not the existence of a classical temporal history.

AI.tldr: Exact no signaling in time (NSIT) does not guarantee classical temporal behavior. Common fixed points of measurement channels can erase marginal evidence of invasiveness while preserving quantum disturbance, leading to NSIT-satisfying states that violate Leggett-Garg inequalities, including the maximally mixed state in a qutrit ring system.
AI.motivation: To challenge the widespread assumption that exact no signaling in time (NSIT) is a sufficient operational indicator of noninvasive measurability and classical temporal behavior.
AI.method: The authors identify common fixed points (CFPs) of nonselective measurement channels as the mechanism that hides invasiveness. They analytically solve the full CFP manifold for a qutrit ring subject to local degenerate Luders measurement, and test NSIT-satisfying states against Leggett-Garg inequalities using hidden variable reconstruction, entropic witnesses, protocol landscape scans, noise robustness, and finite shot simulations.
AI.result: Every state on the CFP manifold satisfies exact pairwise NSIT, yet every nontrivial member (including the maximally mixed state) violates a Leggett-Garg inequality. Violation is governed by finite branch displacement, not residual signaling.
AI.conclusion: Exact NSIT certifies only the disappearance of marginal signals after outcome erasure, not the existence of a classical temporal history. The assumption that NSIT implies classicality is false.

title: Adaptive Entanglement Management in Quantum Multi-Core Architectures
summary: Scalable quantum computing architectures increasingly rely on multi-core designs, where qubits are distributed across multiple processing cores interconnected through a quantum Network-on-Chip (NoC). In such systems, inter-core communication is typically realized through entanglement-assisted quantum teleportation, making efficient entanglement generation critical for performance. In this paper, we perform a comparative study of three entanglement management paradigms for multi-core quantum processors: reactive on-demand generation (ODG), proactive continuous pre-generation (CGP), and an adaptive continuous pre-generation approach (ACGP). While ODG generates entanglement only when required, CGP reduces average teleportation latency by pre-generating EPR pairs in the background. To improve upon this, we propose ACGP which dynamically adjusts entanglement generation probabilities based on observed inter-core communication patterns. We evaluate these approaches using an extended SeQUeNCe simulator on mesh-based multi-core architectures on real benchmark circuits. Results show that ACGP significantly reduces average teleportation latency compared to ODG and CGP. Although pre-generation introduces fidelity degradation due to storage time, entanglement purification effectively restores fidelity with minimal impact on latency. These results demonstrate that adaptive entanglement managements can substantially improve communication efficiency in scalable quantum multi-core systems.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three entanglement management paradigms (ODG, CGP, ACGP) for multi-core quantum processors and proposes an adaptive approach (ACGP) that dynamically adjusts entanglement generation based on communication patterns, significantly reducing teleportation latency in mesh-based architectures.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computing architectures increasingly rely on multi-core designs with quantum NoCs, where efficient entanglement generation is critical for inter-core communication via quantum teleportation. The paper aims to improve communication efficiency in such systems.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative study of three entanglement management paradigms: reactive on-demand generation (ODG), proactive continuous pre-generation (CGP), and an adaptive continuous pre-generation approach (ACGP) that dynamically adjusts entanglement generation probabilities based on observed inter-core communication patterns. Evaluation is conducted using an extended SeQUeNCe simulator on mesh-based multi-core architectures with real benchmark circuits.
AI.result: ACGP significantly reduces average teleportation latency compared to ODG and CGP. Although pre-generation introduces fidelity degradation due to storage time, entanglement purification effectively restores fidelity with minimal impact on latency.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive entanglement management (ACGP) can substantially improve communication efficiency in scalable quantum multi-core systems.

title: Emergence and Recovery of (logical) Kochen-Specker Contextuality via Hamilton Extension
summary: Logical Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality is widely regarded as an intrinsic property of specially constructed measurement configurations. We show instead that it can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets through a constructive procedure we call the Hamilton extension. Defined for four-dimensional vector sets, the Hamilton extension associates each real vector with a measurement context while inducing additional measurement contexts among Hamilton-extended children of distinct parent vectors. These emergent contexts fundamentally alter the compatibility structure, transforming KS-colorable configurations into KS-uncolorable ones and recovering logical contextuality lost under apex-vertex augmentation. We establish a sharp and optimal threshold -- the Hamilton extension of every five-vector parent set remains KS-colorable, whereas suitably chosen six-vector parent sets already generate logical KS contradictions. Thus, six vectors constitute the smallest parent set capable of generating KS contradiction through this mechanism. Our results reveal a new structural route to contextuality, provide a systematic framework for constructing compact KS sets, and have implications for contextuality-based quantum information protocols and graph-theoretic approaches to nonclassicality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Hamilton extension, a procedure that transforms KS-colorable vector sets into KS-uncolorable ones, establishing that six vectors is the minimum parent set size required to generate logical KS contextuality through this mechanism.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing view that KS contextuality is an intrinsic property of specially constructed measurement configurations, and instead show it can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets via a constructive procedure.
AI.method: The Hamilton extension procedure is defined for four-dimensional real vector sets, where each parent vector is associated with a measurement context and induces additional contexts among its "children" (extended vectors), thereby altering the compatibility structure.
AI.result: A sharp threshold is established: the Hamilton extension of every five-vector parent set remains KS-colorable, while suitably chosen six-vector parent sets generate logical KS contradictions. This identifies six vectors as the minimal parent set size for generating KS contextuality via this mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals a new structural route to contextuality, provides a systematic framework for constructing compact KS sets, and has implications for contextuality-based quantum information and graph-theoretic approaches to nonclassicality.

title: Worst-Case Quantum Algorithm for Optimal Polynomial Intersection Beyond Decoded Quantum Interferometry
summary:
The Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem asks us to find a low-degree polynomial over a finite field whose values lie in prescribed subsets on as many given inputs as possible. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) gives a quantum algorithm for OPI in parameter regimes beyond those achieved by the best known classical heuristics. Follow-up works improve the parameter regimes, but their analyses are limited to average-case settings. Recently, Sun and Wootters showed that, even in the worst case, OPI has a solution in a larger parameter regime than the one covered by DQI. However, they left open whether one can design a quantum algorithm that solves OPI in the worst-case beyond the DQI regime.
  We give such a quantum algorithm. As a byproduct, we also improve the existential bound of Sun and Wootters in certain parameter regimes. In particular, when each subset contains roughly half of the field elements, our algorithm finds a solution with satisfaction rate $s=1$ whenever the rate satisfies $R>0.75$. This matches the previous average-case bound, whereas DQI cannot achieve $s=1$ unless $R=1$. Our existential bound guarantees the existence of a solution when $R> 0.7158$, improving over the previous threshold $R>0.7495$. More generally, our existential results extend to the Max-LINSAT problem with respect to arbitrary maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. The corresponding algorithmic results apply only to MDS codes whose dual admits an efficient list decoder. Our results are obtained through a novel application of a Brascamp--Lieb-type inequality in the MDS setting, which may have further applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum algorithm that solves the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem in worst-case parameter regimes beyond what previous quantum algorithms (DQI) could achieve. It also improves existential bounds for OPI and extends results to the Max-LINSAT problem with MDS codes, using a novel Brascamp-Lieb-type inequality.
AI.motivation: Sun and Wootters showed that worst-case OPI has a solution in a larger parameter regime than DQI, but left open whether a quantum algorithm could actually solve it in that regime. This work closes that gap.
AI.method: The algorithm uses a novel application of a Brascamp-Lieb-type inequality in the MDS setting. For the existential results, the approach extends to Max-LINSAT with arbitrary MDS codes; algorithmically, it applies to MDS codes whose dual admits an efficient list decoder.
AI.result: When each subset contains roughly half of the field elements, the algorithm achieves satisfaction rate s=1 whenever the rate R>0.75 (matching average-case bound, while DQI requires R=1). The existential bound improves from R>0.7495 to R>0.7158.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first quantum algorithm for worst-case OPI beyond the DQI regime, improves existential bounds, and introduces a mathematical technique (Brascamp-Lieb-type inequality) with potential for broader applications.

title: Tuning the universality class of a quantum process by Trotterization
summary: We numerically analyze a discretized version of the quantum contact process, a non-equilibrium model having a competition between a coherent infection process and a dissipative recovery process. Previously, the continuous-time version has been discussed to have a phase transition in a novel quantum universality class, while experimental investigations of a related process have pointed towards the transition being in the classical directed percolation class. We demonstrate that these differences stem from details of the discretization of the process and construct a systematic way to continuously interpolate between these results. Finally, we provide evidence that the modification of the universality class is due to destructive interference effects, showing a clear quantum-mechanical origin.

AI.tldr: A numerical analysis of a discretized quantum contact process reveals that differences in universality class (novel quantum vs. classical directed percolation) arise from discretization details, with a systematic interpolation constructed; the class modification is attributed to destructive interference effects of quantum-mechanical origin.
AI.motivation: To resolve discrepancies between previous continuous-time quantum contact process studies (predicting a novel quantum universality class) and experimental investigations (pointing to classical directed percolation), by examining the role of discretization.
AI.method: Numerical analysis of a discretized version of the quantum contact process, with systematic interpolation between discretization schemes.
AI.result: Differences in universality class stem from discretization details; destructive interference effects are identified as the quantum-mechanical origin of the class modification.
AI.conclusion: The apparent discrepancy between quantum and classical universality classes is resolved by considering discretization, and the quantum-class transition is driven by destructive interference.

title: Electrons Hopping across a Molecular Network: Spectra and Symmetries
comment: submitted to special issue in Physics: "Quantum Theory 100 Years Later: advances on Foundations and Applications"
summary: We investigate interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular ring networks described by a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian. The interplay between lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions and discrete symmetries is analysed for rings with $L=3,4,5,6$ nodes, filled with one, two or three electrons. Special attention is devoted to the role of the network symmetries in determining the structure of the many-body spectrum and the Mulliken classification of the eigenstates. Using group-theoretical methods, we examine the evolution of the spectra in the presence of an external magnetic flux. The Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and results in combination with the Coulomb interaction to avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. We identify a qualitatively distinction between systems with an even and odd number of particles. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.

AI.tldr: A group-theoretical study of interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular rings (L=3-6) using the Hubbard model, examining how lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions, and discrete symmetries shape the many-body spectrum under magnetic flux, with particle-hole symmetry protecting certain sectors at half-filling.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions, and discrete symmetries in finite molecular ring networks, particularly how network symmetries determine the many-body spectrum structure and eigenstate classification under an external magnetic field.
AI.method: Tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian for spinless electrons on finite rings with L=3,4,5,6 nodes, filled with 1-3 electrons. Group-theoretical methods to analyze spectra under magnetic flux. Mulliken classification of eigenstates based on network symmetries.
AI.result: Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and, combined with Coulomb interaction, produces avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. A qualitative distinction exists between even and odd particle numbers. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.
AI.conclusion: Particle-hole symmetry provides protection of certain symmetry sectors from Zeeman splitting at half-filling, revealing a symmetry-driven robustness in finite molecular ring systems with even particle numbers.

title: High-rate continuous-variable quantum key distribution coexisting with Tb/s coherent classical transmission in hollow-core fiber
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) can provide secret keys with security rooted in quantum mechanics, but operation alongside high-capacity classical traffic remains limited by the excess-noise budget of weak quantum states in conventional solid-core fiber. Here, we combine ultralow-loss anti-resonant hollow-core fiber with residual-carrier-assisted discrete-modulation continuous-variable QKD (DM-CV-QKD) to address both propagation-induced coexistence noise and low-SNR phase recovery. Over a 24.3-km hollow-core link with 3.3-dB end-to-end loss, a dual-polarization 15-Gbaud DM-CV-QKD channel achieves an average asymptotic secret-key rate (SKR) of 153.22 Mb/s and a finite-size SKR of 149.99 Mb/s, while 39 coherent wavelength-division-multiplexed channels deliver an aggregate data rate of 7.6 Tb/s and a net data rate of 7.2 Tb/s. The system can even sustain a positive SKR under a high classical launch power of up to 15 dBm, without an optical bandpass filter (BPF). Finite-size analysis against collective attacks further yields a projected positive secret-key rate at a 100-km-equivalent condition. These results show that an anti-resonant hollow-core fiber, combined with carrier-assisted phase recovery, can greatly extend the operating regime of shared-fiber quantum-secured coherent links, pointing to a promising approach for integrating high-rate CV-QKD with high-capacity optical networks.

AI.tldr: Combining anti-resonant hollow-core fiber with carrier-assisted DM-CV-QKD, the paper demonstrates a 24.3-km link achieving 153 Mb/s asymptotic SKR and 149.99 Mb/s finite-size SKR, coexisting with 7.6 Tb/s classical traffic, with positive SKR sustained even at 15 dBm classical launch power and projected at 100-km-equivalent distances.
AI.motivation: Conventional solid-core fiber limits QKD's coexistence with high-capacity classical traffic due to excess noise from Raman scattering and nonlinear effects on weak quantum states.
AI.method: Ultralow-loss anti-resonant hollow-core fiber is combined with residual-carrier-assisted discrete-modulation continuous-variable QKD (DM-CV-QKD) to reduce propagation-induced noise and improve low-SNR phase recovery.
AI.result: Over 24.3 km (3.3 dB loss): asymptotic SKR = 153.22 Mb/s, finite-size SKR = 149.99 Mb/s; coexisting classical channels achieve 7.6 Tb/s aggregate and 7.2 Tb/s net data rate; positive SKR up to 15 dBm classical launch power without BPF; projected positive SKR at 100-km-equivalent condition.
AI.conclusion: Anti-resonant hollow-core fiber with carrier-assisted phase recovery greatly extends the operating regime of shared-fiber quantum-secured coherent links, enabling high-rate CV-QKD integration with high-capacity optical networks.

title: Moment Optimization in the Navascués-Pironio-Acín Hierarchy
summary:
The Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy provides a convergent sequence of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for noncommutative polynomial optimisation, ubiquitous in quantum physics. However, its practical applicability is limited by the combinatorial growth in operator moments required at each level. Since not all moments contribute equally to bound tightness, selecting moments within a fixed computational budget is a relevant problem.
  We reframe moment selection as combinatorial subset selection and show it is governed by strong higher-order synergistic interactions among moments, quantified through a marginal synergy diagnostic adapted from complex systems theory. We develop and compare three optimisation methods: Parallel Tempering (PT), an RBM-based reinforcement learning policy, and Bayesian Optimisation (BO). On the $I_{3322}$ Bell inequality benchmark, all three substantially outperform greedy approaches at costs around two orders of magnitude below brute force, with the RBM achieving the closest approach to optimal throughout the hard transition regime.
  We apply the framework to the 174 Bell inequalities in the $(4,4,2,2)$ scenario, finding heterogeneous convergence behaviour across inequalities, and to the one-dimensional Heisenberg spin chain, demonstrating that physically motivated monomial bases are internally compressible and are not globally optimal in general. A budget-aware search over a broader pool improves certified bounds on long-range correlations by nearly two orders of magnitude. These results establish a scalable framework for moment selection in noncommutative polynomial optimisation, with broad applications across quantum physics and quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes moment selection in the NPA hierarchy as a combinatorial subset selection problem, demonstrates strong synergistic interactions among moments, develops three optimisation methods (PT, RBM-based RL, BO) that outperform greedy approaches, and applies the framework to Bell inequalities and the Heisenberg spin chain, showing significant improvements in certified bounds.
AI.motivation: The NPA hierarchy provides convergent SDP relaxations for noncommutative polynomial optimisation but is limited by combinatorial growth of operator moments. Selecting the most impactful moments within a fixed computational budget is a critical open problem.
AI.method: Moment selection is reframed as combinatorial subset selection with a marginal synergy diagnostic from complex systems theory. Three optimisation methods are developed: Parallel Tempering (PT), RBM-based reinforcement learning, and Bayesian Optimisation (BO).
AI.result: On the I3322 Bell inequality benchmark, all three methods substantially outperform greedy approaches at ~2 orders of magnitude below brute force, with the RBM achieving closest-to-optimal performance. Applied to 174 Bell inequalities in the (4,4,2,2) scenario and the 1D Heisenberg spin chain, the framework improves certified bounds on long-range correlations by nearly two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a scalable framework for moment selection in noncommutative polynomial optimisation, demonstrating that physically motivated monomial bases are internally compressible and not globally optimal, with broad applications across quantum physics and quantum information.

title: Robustness of periodicity in Grover walks under a magnetic vector potential
summary: We study the effect of magnetic vector potentials on periodic Grover walks on finite graphs. The magnetic vector potential is introduced through the framework of quantum graphs, which induces the Grover walk as a special case. We regard the vector potential as a perturbation of a periodic Grover walk and investigate the robustness of its periodicity. Our analysis reveals that the response to such perturbations depends on the spectral structure of the underlying graph. In particular, when the graph possesses at least one non-simple eigenvalue, we derive a Hermitian matrix that characterizes the robustness of its periodicity. As a consequence, we show that the perturbed dynamics is asymptotically described by a continuous-time quantum walk generated by this Hermitian matrix.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how magnetic vector potentials perturb periodic Grover walks on finite graphs, finding that robustness depends on the graph's spectral structure, with non-simple eigenvalues leading to a Hermitian matrix that asymptotically describes a continuous-time quantum walk.
AI.motivation: To understand the effect of magnetic vector potentials on periodic Grover walks and investigate the robustness of periodicity under such perturbations.
AI.method: The magnetic vector potential is introduced via quantum graph frameworks, inducing the Grover walk as a special case. The vector potential is treated as a perturbation, and a Hermitian matrix characterizing robustness is derived for graphs with at least one non-simple eigenvalue.
AI.result: The response to perturbations depends on the spectral structure; for graphs with non-simple eigenvalues, a Hermitian matrix characterizes periodicity robustness, and the perturbed dynamics asymptotically becomes a continuous-time quantum walk generated by this matrix.
AI.conclusion: The periodicity of Grover walks under magnetic perturbations is governed by the graph's spectral properties, leading to an asymptotic continuous-time quantum walk description.

title: Quantum Remote Implementation of Hybrid Operations on Hyperstates Using Hyperentangled States
summary: Quantum remote control, also known as quantum remote implementation of an operator (QRIO), enables the remote manipulation of an arbitrary quantum state by implementing a desired quantum operation at a distant location. Significant progress has recently been made in developing QRIO protocols and their variants. Most existing schemes employ hyperentangled states where entanglement is shared across multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs). However, these protocols typically exploit only one degree of freedom at a time. In this work, we propose a QRIO protocol that simultaneously utilizes the polarization and spatial DOFs of a two-qubit hyperentangled state to remotely implement an arbitrary hybrid operator on an unknown single-photon two-qubit hyperstate. The shared hyperentangled resource is realized using the polarization and spatial modes of photons, while the protocol is constructed using linear optical elements and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions to facilitate effective photon-photon coupling. Furthermore, the effects of measurement errors arising from finite coherent state distinguishability and coherent state dissipation are analyzed and the corresponding success probability of the protocol is evaluated. The results demonstrate that an appropriate choice of the cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude significantly enhances the protocol performance, making the proposed scheme a promising candidate for hybrid quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum remote control (QRIO) protocol that simultaneously uses both polarization and spatial degrees of freedom of a two-qubit hyperentangled state to remotely implement arbitrary hybrid operators on single-photon two-qubit hyperstates, using linear optics and cross-Kerr nonlinearities, with analysis of measurement errors and success probability.
AI.motivation: Existing QRIO protocols typically exploit only one degree of freedom at a time despite using hyperentangled states; this work aims to simultaneously utilize multiple DOFs (polarization and spatial) for more efficient remote operator implementation.
AI.method: The protocol employs a two-qubit hyperentangled state shared across polarization and spatial modes of photons, using linear optical elements and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions for photon-photon coupling, and analyzes measurement errors from finite coherent state distinguishability and dissipation.
AI.result: Appropriate choice of cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude significantly enhances protocol performance, with quantified success probability under measurement errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme is a promising candidate for hybrid quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

title: Binary Gauss Stabilizers for Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories
summary: Gauge theories and quantum error-correcting codes share the same underlying structure: both use constraints to identify a specific subspace of the full Hilbert space. In quantum error correction, these constraints are known as stabilizers, while in gauge theories they correspond to Gauss law. In this work, we consider a family of discrete Abelian lattice gauge theories described by a $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ gauge group with $N$ an arbitrary power of two. In this setting, we find a set of stabilizers for the gauge-invariant subspace which is an alternative to the Gauss operators, and we call them binary Gauss stabilizers. We use this alternative stabilizer group to build practical error-correcting codes exploiting the gauge symmetries of the system without the addition of extra qubits. The applications of our finding are not limited to error correction though. We also provide a new strategy of gauge fixing to remove the redundancies based on our alternative stabilizer, which might provide advantages with respect to already-existing approaches such as the axial gauge. Our results provide new tools to study lattice gauge theories and their quantum simulation, and opens directions for future work at the interface of lattice gauge theory and quantum information.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a formal connection between gauge theories and quantum error-correcting codes by identifying binary Gauss stabilizers as an alternative stabilizer set for discrete Abelian lattice gauge theories (Z_N, N a power of two), enabling code construction without extra qubits and offering a new gauge-fixing strategy.
AI.motivation: To unify the underlying constraint structure of gauge theories and quantum error correction, and to leverage this connection for practical code construction and improved gauge-fixing methods in lattice gauge theories.
AI.method: The authors consider discrete Abelian lattice gauge theories with Z_N gauge group (N a power of two), identify binary Gauss stabilizers as an alternative to standard Gauss-law operators for the gauge-invariant subspace, use these stabilizers to build quantum error-correcting codes without additional qubits, and propose a new gauge-fixing strategy based on these stabilizers.
AI.result: A set of binary Gauss stabilizers that characterize the gauge-invariant subspace; a method to construct practical quantum error-correcting codes directly from the gauge symmetries; a new gauge-fixing approach that may outperform existing methods like axial gauge.
AI.conclusion: The work provides new cross-disciplinary tools for lattice gauge theory and quantum information, with implications for quantum simulation and error correction, and opens future directions at the interface of these fields.

title: Limits on Broadcasting Genuine Multipartite Entanglement in Quantum Networks
comment: 4 pages (double column) + 12 pages (single column), 6 figure; Comments are welcome
summary: We establish operational limits on the broadcasting of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in quantum networks. Using a distributed protocol in which each of N parties locally implements optimal 1 $\to$ 2 cloning via beam-splitter interactions, we derive exact expressions for the broadcast fidelity of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), W states, and Cluster states in a limited setting. We show that the fidelity decays exponentially with system size as [c(R)]$^N$, providing a quantitative expression of multipartite entanglement monogamy in the broadcasting setting, and that both state families share a universal normalisation factor arising from independent post-selection probabilities. Most significantly, we prove a no-go result for simultaneous GME certification: for all reflectivities and all system sizes, the two broadcast copies cannot be simultaneously certified as genuinely multipartite entangled within the standard framework of fidelity-based witnesses. We further check this behaviour for three- and four-party cluster states, finding consistent results that support the generality of the no-go beyond the GHZ and W families. This obstruction arises from the redistribution of multipartite coherence, which both reduces the achievable fidelity and increases the corresponding certification threshold. Our results reveal a fundamental trade-off between the broadcastability of multipartite entanglement and its operational certifiability, and delineate intrinsic limits on entanglement distribution in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes fundamental limits on broadcasting genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in quantum networks. For N parties using optimal 1→2 cloning via beam-splitters, broadcast fidelity decays exponentially as [c(R)]^N for GHZ, W, and Cluster states. Crucially, it proves a no-go result: the two broadcast copies cannot be simultaneously certified as GME using fidelity-based witnesses, due to redistribution of multipartite coherence. This reveals a fundamental trade-off between broadcastability and certifiability of multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: To understand fundamental limits on distributing and broadcasting genuine multipartite entanglement in quantum networks, particularly exploring the trade-off between entanglement broadcastability and operational certifiability.
AI.method: The authors derive exact analytic expressions for broadcast fidelity of GHZ, W, and Cluster states under a protocol where N parties locally implement optimal 1→2 cloning via beam-splitter interactions. They analyze fidelity decay with system size and study simultaneous GME certification using fidelity-based witnesses across different reflectivities and system sizes.
AI.result: Broadcast fidelity decays exponentially as [c(R)]^N; a universal normalization factor from independent post-selection probabilities exists across state families; a no-go result shows two broadcast copies cannot be simultaneously certified as GME within standard fidelity-based witness framework; this holds for GHZ, W, and Cluster states, suggesting generality.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between the broadcastability of multipartite entanglement and its operational certifiability, revealing intrinsic limits on entanglement distribution in quantum networks arising from multipartite coherence redistribution.

title: A Geometric Theory of Fermion-to-Qubit Encodings
summary: Exact fermion to qubit transformations are conventionally regarded as algorithmic tools that translate many-body Hamiltonians into qubit representations for quantum simulation. Here we show that they also define intrinsic geometric representations whose structure encodes physically meaningful information beyond spectral equivalence. We develop a geometric framework based on weighted hypergraphs and coupling space representations constructed from the Bravyi--Kitaev (BK) and Xia--Bian--Kais (XBK) encodings. Within the BK representation, we introduce a geometric observable that compares the algebraic connectivities of the kinetic and interaction hypergraphs, derive its exact analytical dependence on interaction strength, and uncover two geometric universality classes together with an exact spectral organization originating from the binary tree architecture of the encoding. The complementary XBK representation describes the evolution of encoded Hamiltonians through probability measures in coupling space, where optimal transport quantifies interaction-driven reorganization independently of the spectral analysis. Applications to the Hubbard, spinless tV , single impurity Anderson, and Kitaev models demonstrate that these connectivity and transport based geometric descriptions consistently capture the structural evolution of encoded quantum Hamiltonians across distinct classes of many-body systems. Our results establish hypergraph geometry as a new framework for understanding fermion-to-qubit encodings,revealing that they serve not only as computational mappings but also as geometric representations of quantum many-body Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: Fermion-to-qubit transformations define intrinsic geometric representations (via weighted hypergraphs and coupling spaces) that reveal physically meaningful structure beyond spectral equivalence. Using BK and XBK encodings, the paper introduces geometric observables, identifies universality classes, and applies optimal transport to analyze encoded Hamiltonians across Hubbard, tV, Anderson, and Kitaev models.
AI.motivation: To show that fermion-to-qubit encodings are not merely algorithmic tools for quantum simulation but also define geometric representations that encode physically meaningful information beyond spectral equivalence.
AI.method: Develops a geometric framework using weighted hypergraphs and coupling space representations from BK and XBK encodings. Introduces a geometric observable comparing algebraic connectivities of kinetic/interaction hypergraphs, derives analytical dependence on interaction strength, and uses optimal transport in coupling space for the XBK representation.
AI.result: Identifies two geometric universality classes and an exact spectral organization from the binary tree structure of BK encoding. The XBK representation quantifies interaction-driven reorganization via optimal transport. Applications to Hubbard, spinless tV, single impurity Anderson, and Kitaev models show connectivity and transport-based descriptions consistently capture structural evolution across distinct many-body systems.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph geometry provides a new framework for understanding fermion-to-qubit encodings, revealing that they serve as both computational mappings and geometric representations of quantum many-body Hamiltonians.

title: Evolution-Level Quantum Optimal Control of Single-Qubit Gates with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Quantum gate design is often represented as pulse optimization, although the physical object that implements a gate is the full controlled evolution generated by the pulse. Here we use physics-informed neural networks to represent single-qubit gate design at this evolution level: the control fields, the Bloch-state trajectories, and the total duration are learned together under the Bloch equation. This changes the optimized object from pulse amplitudes to a differentiable physical process whose structure can be inspected and refined. For rotation gates, the optimized evolutions recover the physical organization expected for bounded single-qubit control, with no prescribed pulse ansatz or duration scan. For a geometric gate, the representation identifies localized bottlenecks in maintaining the geometric condition and turns this diagnosis into feedback, reducing the residual path error while preserving high fidelity. Thus physics-informed learning is used not only to synthesize gates, but also to make optimized quantum controls physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable. This process-level view may be especially useful for adapting gates to hardware-specific, task-specific, and locally varying experimental constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper uses physics-informed neural networks to design single-qubit quantum gates at the evolution level, jointly learning control fields, Bloch-state trajectories, and gate duration under the Bloch equation, enabling physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable gate synthesis.
AI.motivation: Quantum gate design is typically formulated as pulse optimization, but the actual physical object implementing a gate is the full controlled evolution. The authors aim to redesign the optimization at this process level to improve interpretability and diagnosability.
AI.method: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are used to represent single-qubit gate design, where control fields, Bloch-state trajectories, and total duration are jointly learned under the constraint of the Bloch equation.
AI.result: For rotation gates, the optimized evolutions recover the expected physical organization for bounded single-qubit control without prescribed pulse ansatz or duration scanning. For geometric gates, the method identifies localized bottlenecks in maintaining the geometric condition, enabling feedback that reduces residual path error while preserving high fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed learning can not only synthesize quantum gates but also make optimized controls physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable. This process-level view is particularly useful for adapting gates to hardware-specific, task-specific, and locally varying experimental constraints.

title: A Three-Point Continuous-Variable Quantum MacWilliams Identity
comment: 35 pages. Ancillary files: positive-definite certificates for the CP collapse theorem (JSON, N=1 exact-rational and N=2 floating-point) and a stdlib-only exact verification script (anc/)
summary: We construct the three-point continuous-variable (CV) quantum MacWilliams identity, extending the two-point framework of Burchards, and give its closed-form integral kernel. Its configuration space carries a symplectic invariant with no classical counterpart, which encodes the GKP quantization condition and a three-point sign phase. Using the identity, we derive the semidefinite-programming bounds it supports on the dimension of CV quantum error-correcting codes, and we prove, in two collapse theorems, that the three-point apparatus does not improve on the two-point bound. For GKP lattice codes the three-point optimum equals the Burchards two-point linear-programming optimum identically. This is an exact determination of the lattice three-point optimum, so the $E_8$ and Leech magic functions saturate it rather than beat it. For general bosonic codes a completely-positive reformulation bypasses the positivity obstruction that rules out the natural factored-form constructions; the phase-sign condition together with Choi positivity then force the three-point term to vanish. We certify this collapse for radial Choi forms on the first eight Laguerre levels at one mode, and leave the full trace-class cone open. Both collapses have a single cause with no classical analogue, the code projector: it orients the bound correctly but also removes the full positivity that powers the classical three-point improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a three-point continuous-variable quantum MacWilliams identity, derives semidefinite-programming bounds for CV quantum error-correcting codes, and proves two collapse theorems showing that the three-point framework does not improve on the two-point bound—due to the code projector's orienting effect that removes full positivity.
AI.motivation: To extend the two-point CV quantum MacWilliams identity to three points, study its symplectic invariants, and explore whether the three-point framework can yield tighter bounds on the dimension of CV quantum error-correcting codes.
AI.method: Constructs the three-point CV quantum MacWilliams identity with a closed-form integral kernel; uses semidefinite programming to derive bounds; proves two collapse theorems analyzing the three-point bound relative to the two-point bound; applies the framework to GKP lattice codes and general bosonic codes with a completely-positive reformulation.
AI.result: The three-point apparatus does not improve on the two-point bound; for GKP lattice codes the three-point optimum equals the two-point linear-programming optimum; the E8 and Leech magic functions saturate rather than beat it; for general bosonic codes, the phase-sign condition plus Choi positivity forces the three-point term to vanish; collapse is certified for radial Choi forms on the first eight Laguerre levels at one mode.
AI.conclusion: Both collapses stem from a single cause with no classical analogue: the code projector orients the bound correctly but also removes the full positivity that powers classical three-point improvement.

title: Strong $O$-valued contextuality: ruling out discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory
summary: Gleason's theorem identifies the Born rule via non-contextuality over an infinite continuous lattice of projectors, while its corollary the Kochen-Specker (KS) theorem rules out the specific class of deterministic ($\{0,1\}$-valued) noncontextual models using finite sets of projectors. Gleason's theorem also indicates the existence of KS-type finite vector constructions to rule out other discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory beyond the $\{0, 1\}$ case. Here, we construct finite measurement configurations to rule out noncontextual empirical models with outcome probabilities drawn from an arbitrary finite subset $O \subset [0,1]$. We do this by two means: (i) constructing a family of experimentally feasible state-dependent Hardy-type tests, and (ii) proving a generalized KS theorem for a broad class of $O$ that includes prior results as special cases. In the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger, a hierarchy of probabilistic-possibilistic-strong contextuality has been established quantifying contextuality as a resource. We extend this framework by introducing strong $O$-valued contextuality, showing that quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves. We also discuss the implications of the result on finite many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum theory and for contextuality-based (semi)-device-independent protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs finite measurement configurations that rule out noncontextual empirical models where outcome probabilities come from any arbitrary finite subset O ⊂ [0,1], extending Gleason's and Kochen-Specker theorems. It does so via (i) Hardy-type state-dependent tests and (ii) a generalized KS theorem, and introduces strong O-valued contextuality within the sheaf-theoretic framework.
AI.motivation: To extend contextuality no-go theorems beyond deterministic (0,1-valued) and full probabilistic cases to any finite-valued outcome probability set, and to understand the implications for finite many-valued logics as ontological models for quantum theory.
AI.method: (i) Constructing experimentally feasible state-dependent Hardy-type tests for ruling out noncontextual models with arbitrary finite outcome probability sets O. (ii) Proving a generalized Kochen-Specker theorem for a broad class of O. (iii) Extending the sheaf-theoretic framework by introducing strong O-valued contextuality.
AI.result: Quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves, meaning noncontextual models with outcome probabilities from any finite subset O ⊂ [0,1] are ruled out. This includes prior results as special cases.
AI.conclusion: The results have implications for finite many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum theory and for contextuality-based (semi-)device-independent protocols.

title: Pareto-optimal work extraction and the thermodynamic cost of precision in quantum information engines
summary: We study a finite-time quantum information engine in which a two-level system is measured by a quantum harmonic oscillator acting as a meter and where useful work is extracted conditionally on the measurement outcome. Using multi-objective optimisation, we find a Pareto-optimal trade-off between extractable work and its fluctuations and show that reducing fluctuations entails higher thermodynamic costs: greater information consumption, more engine cycles, longer operation time, and reduced average work output. In the limit of a highly accurate meter, we obtain the work distribution, its moments, and the Pareto front analytically. In this regime, the work statistics of the engine reduce to those of a qubit in contact with a single thermal bath. We further analyse the associated information flows by examining the mutual information and Fisher information, and show that the Pareto-optimal engine designs lie very close to local maxima of the latter with respect to the operation time of the device. Our results provide a compact description of the trade-offs between work, its fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines.

AI.tldr: A finite-time quantum information engine using a two-level system measured by a harmonic oscillator is studied, revealing Pareto-optimal trade-offs between extractable work and fluctuations, with higher costs for reduced fluctuations. Analytical results for work distribution and Pareto front are derived in the high-accuracy limit, showing equivalence to a qubit in a thermal bath.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental trade-offs between work extraction, fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines operating under finite-time, measurement-based feedback control.
AI.method: Multi-objective optimization to find Pareto-optimal trade-offs; analytical derivation of work distribution, moments, and Pareto front in the highly accurate meter limit; analysis of mutual and Fisher information.
AI.result: Reducing fluctuations requires higher thermodynamic costs (more information, more cycles, longer time, less average work). In the high-accuracy limit, work statistics reduce to a qubit in a single thermal bath. Pareto-optimal designs lie near local Fisher information maxima.
AI.conclusion: Compact description of trade-offs between work, fluctuations, and costs in quantum information engines is achieved, with Pareto-optimal designs closely linked to Fisher information maxima.

title: Implicit differentiation of tensor network algorithms
summary: The current leading approach to the variational optimization of projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) is based on automatic differentiation, which allows for a convenient evaluation of the energy gradient with respect to the local variational degrees of freedom. However, evaluating the energy gradient not only remains a major computational bottleneck of the optimization procedure, but also suffers from frequent numerical instabilities. In this work, we adopt recent advances in implicit differentiation techniques to address these challenges in PEPS optimization. By reformulating the core step of the gradient computation in terms of a single characteristic equation for the contraction environment, we reduce the cost of the gradient computation and improve its scaling with the problem size. By choosing a suitable parametrization of this characteristic equation based on the intrinsic symmetries of the contraction environment, we can directly remove instabilities from the global gradient computation that would otherwise arise from the derivatives of subroutines of the contraction algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate how this approach drastically simplifies the practical implementation of stable gradient-based PEPS optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper improves variational optimization of projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) by using implicit differentiation to reduce computational cost, improve scaling, and eliminate numerical instabilities in gradient computation.
AI.motivation: Current PEPS optimization using automatic differentiation suffers from high computational cost and frequent numerical instabilities in energy gradient evaluation.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the gradient computation using implicit differentiation, reducing it to a single characteristic equation for the contraction environment, and parametrize this equation using intrinsic symmetries to remove instabilities.
AI.result: The approach reduces the cost and improves scaling of gradient computation with problem size, and eliminates numerical instabilities arising from subroutines of the contraction algorithm.
AI.conclusion: This method drastically simplifies the practical implementation of stable gradient-based PEPS optimization.

title: Machine-Learning-Empowered Quantum Sensing of the Plaquette Phase in a Three-Level Delta System
summary: We propose a machine-learning-empowered approach to the quantum sensing of the plaquette phase, a gauge-invariant quantity arising in three-level $Δ$ systems. This phase profoundly affects the system dynamics, breaking coherent population trapping and inducing a non-trivial phase dependence of the dynamics. We demonstrate that a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), trained in a supervised-learning framework, can accurately estimate the plaquette phase from STImulated Raman Adiabatic Passage (STIRAP) population transfer efficiencies measured under different driving conditions, which provide experimentally accessible observables. Our results highlight how the combination of coherent control and machine learning (ML) enables effective phase identification in closed-loop quantum systems, opening new perspectives for quantum technologies, specifically quantum sensing applications including synthetic gauge fields.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a machine-learning approach using a multi-layer perceptron to estimate the plaquette phase (a gauge-invariant quantity in three-level Δ systems) from STIRAP population transfer efficiencies, demonstrating effective quantum sensing for synthetic gauge fields.
AI.motivation: The plaquette phase is a gauge-invariant quantity that profoundly affects system dynamics by breaking coherent population trapping and inducing non-trivial phase dependence; however, it is not directly experimentally accessible, motivating the need for an estimation method.
AI.method: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) was trained using supervised learning on STIRAP population transfer efficiencies measured under different driving conditions, which serve as experimentally accessible observables.
AI.result: The MLP accurately estimates the plaquette phase from the STIRAP population transfer data, demonstrating effective phase identification in closed-loop quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The combination of coherent control and machine learning enables effective quantum sensing of the plaquette phase, opening new perspectives for quantum technologies and synthetic gauge field applications.

title: Towards logical entanglement creation in trivalent planar architectures
summary: Low-overhead quantum error-correction schemes are essential for enabling quantum computation on registers containing multiple logical qubits. For planar architectures with limited nearest-neighbor qubit connectivity, the surface code has emerged as the leading paradigm. Recent theoretical and experimental work has shown that a physical-qubit connectivity of degree three is sufficient to implement fault-tolerant quantum error correction. In this work, we study lattice surgery in the context of such trivalent architectures and introduce scalable circuit constructions to implement it. Compared with the four-valent measurement scheme, the trivalent lattice-surgery protocol reduces the required resources by $\mathcal{O}(d)$ qubits out of a total qubit count of $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ and by $\mathcal{O}(d)$ two-qubit gates out of a total two-qubit gate count of $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$. We benchmark the logical fidelity of both lattice-surgery schemes in terms of experimentally realistic simulations targeting an implementation with a fluxonium qubit based architecture and find a potential improvement of up to $\approx25\%$ for distance-three. These results open a way for scalable planar trivalent qubit architectures to host a surface-code-based logical quantum processor.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces trivalent (degree-3 connectivity) lattice surgery for surface code quantum error correction, reducing qubit requirements by O(d) and two-qubit gates by O(d) compared to standard four-valent schemes, with up to ~25% logical fidelity improvement for distance-three in fluxonium-based implementations.
AI.motivation: Low-overhead quantum error correction is essential for multi-logical-qubit quantum computation. While the surface code is leading for planar architectures, the standard approach requires four-valent (degree-4) qubit connectivity. Recent work shows degree-3 connectivity suffices for fault-tolerant QEC, but lattice surgery—a critical operation for logical qubit interactions—has not been systematically studied for trivalent architectures.
AI.method: The authors design scalable circuit constructions for lattice surgery on trivalent (degree-3 connectivity) planar qubit architectures. They compare resource requirements (qubit count, two-qubit gate count) against standard four-valent measurement schemes analytically. They also perform experimentally realistic simulations targeting a fluxonium qubit-based architecture to benchmark logical fidelity.
AI.result: The trivalent lattice-surgery protocol reduces required qubits by O(d) out of total O(d²), and reduces two-qubit gates by O(d) out of total O(d³). Logical fidelity simulations for distance-three show a potential improvement of up to ~25% over the four-valent scheme in fluxonium-based architectures.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate a scalable path for planar trivalent qubit architectures to host a surface-code-based logical quantum processor, reducing resource overhead while potentially improving logical fidelity.

title: SQD-Enabled Circuit Compression for Resource-Efficient Quantum Chemistry
comment: Accepted by IEEE/ACM 2026 International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (IEEE/ACM ICCAD 2026)
summary: Subspace Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) recovers ground-state energies by classically diagonalizing a Hamiltonian in the subspace spanned by quantum samples, requiring only bitstrings with sufficient ground-state overlap rather than an accurate variational energy. We reveal and exploit this underexplored robustness property: how much non-Clifford and variational expressivity can be removed from the sampling circuit before SQD accuracy degrades? We answer through two complementary compression techniques: gradient-based operator pruning, which discards low-impact excitation operators, and Clifford rounding, which snaps remaining parameters to the nearest Clifford angle. Both of these techniques can be applied to a VQE ansatz on a qubit-reduced Hamiltonian. A systematic ablation study across 21 molecules shows that median SQD error stays within chemical accuracy even at 50\% compression on both axes, while simulation speedup reaches $33\times$. Hardware validation on 6 molecules on IBM quantum hardware confirms up to $2.8\times$ transpiled-depth reduction with zero loss in SQD accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that Subspace Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) is robust to significant compression of the quantum sampling circuit—pruning low-impact operators and rounding parameters to Clifford angles—achieving up to 33× simulation speedup and 2.8× transpiled-depth reduction on hardware while maintaining chemical accuracy across 21 molecules.
AI.motivation: To exploit the underexplored robustness property of SQD—specifically, how much non-Clifford and variational expressivity can be removed from the sampling circuit before accuracy degrades.
AI.method: Two complementary compression techniques: (1) gradient-based operator pruning to discard low-impact excitation operators, and (2) Clifford rounding to snap remaining parameters to the nearest Clifford angle. Applied to a VQE ansatz on qubit-reduced Hamiltonians and evaluated via systematic ablation on 21 molecules.
AI.result: Median SQD error stays within chemical accuracy at 50% compression on both axes; simulation speedup reaches 33×. Hardware validation on 6 molecules shows up to 2.8× transpiled-depth reduction with zero SQD accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: SQD is remarkably robust to circuit compression, enabling significant computational speedups and hardware savings without sacrificing accuracy in ground-state energy estimation.

title: An experimental pathway towards an exact theory of strong coupling
summary: We employ a mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation to arrive at an exact theoretical description of a two-level system strongly coupled to the environment. The framework, while intuitive, shedding light on the physics of the problem, and agreeing with existing results, such as thermalisation to a non-canonical state, is based around three parameters that are unknown outside of the weak coupling regime -- the analogue to the detailed balance relation, and two coupling strength constants. As a way forward, we propose a feasible experimental protocol based on a solid-state electronic quantum dot device, through which the fundamental parameters of the problem can be revealed, which would further the fundamental understanding of strong coupling.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an exact theoretical description of a two-level system strongly coupled to an environment using a mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation, and proposes an experimental protocol using a quantum dot device to reveal unknown fundamental parameters beyond the weak coupling regime.
AI.motivation: To develop an exact theoretical framework for strong coupling that is intuitive and physically transparent, while addressing the fact that key parameters (detailed balance analogue and coupling strength constants) remain unknown outside the weak coupling regime.
AI.method: A mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation is employed to derive an exact description of a two-level system strongly coupled to the environment, along with a proposed experimental protocol based on a solid-state electronic quantum dot device to measure the unknown parameters.
AI.result: The framework agrees with existing results such as thermalisation to a non-canonical state, and identifies three fundamental parameters (detailed balance analogue and two coupling strength constants) that characterize strong coupling but are currently undetermined outside the weak coupling regime.
AI.conclusion: The proposed experimental protocol could reveal the fundamental parameters, thereby advancing the fundamental understanding of strong coupling physics.

title: Quantum Lock-In Detection via Successive Adiabatic Evolution
summary: In recent years, quantum lock-in detection has emerged as a promising technique to accurately detect weak signals submerged in background noise. However, the signal-to-noise ratio of existing protocols is severely limited by spectral leakage resulting from control operations implemented in pulse form. Here, we propose a general protocol for realizing quantum lock-in detection by employing successive quantum adiabatic evolution. In our protocol, the signal modulation is achieved by adiabatically controlling the time evolution of the quantum probe, which enables the implementation of triangular modulation functions. The realization of triangular-wave modulation fundamentally solves the problem of spectral leakage and facilitates the extraction of the complete characteristics of the target signals. We present a practical implementation scheme of adiabatic quantum lock-in detection based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, and demonstrate that the proposed protocol possesses strong resilience against experimental imperfections. Our results establish adiabatic quantum lock-in detection as a robust and experimentally accessible approach to detection of weak alternating signals in noisy environments, thus promoting the advance of real-world quantum sensing technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adiabatic quantum lock-in detection protocol using triangular-wave modulation to eliminate spectral leakage, enabling robust detection of weak alternating signals in noisy environments, demonstrated with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum lock-in detection protocols suffer from severely limited signal-to-noise ratios due to spectral leakage caused by pulse-form control operations, hindering accurate detection of weak signals in background noise.
AI.method: The protocol employs successive quantum adiabatic evolution to modulate signals by adiabatically controlling the quantum probe's time evolution, implementing triangular modulation functions instead of traditional pulse-based modulation, fundamentally solving spectral leakage.
AI.result: The proposed protocol demonstrates strong resilience against experimental imperfections and enables extraction of complete signal characteristics, with a practical implementation scheme based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond.
AI.conclusion: Adiabatic quantum lock-in detection is established as a robust and experimentally accessible approach for detecting weak alternating signals in noisy environments, advancing real-world quantum sensing technologies.

title: On the origin of finite entanglement scaling
summary: The concept of finite entanglement scaling forms one of the pillars on which the tensor network ecosystem is built. In this paper, we resolve the open problem of determining the actual perturbations induced by matrix product state approximations of critical systems, and we demonstrate that these can be quite different than the ones predicted by conformal field theory. To that aim, we develop a sparse linear solver to calculate the forward and backward derivatives of 2-dimensional tensor networks with respect to their defining parameters in an implicit way. This algorithm is of independent interest as it provides a primitive for the variational optimization of projected entangled pair states that circumvents the instabilities plaguing traditional automatic differentiation methods.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the open problem of determining perturbations from matrix product state approximations of critical systems, showing they differ from conformal field theory predictions, and develops a sparse linear solver for implicit derivatives of 2D tensor networks that improves variational optimization of PEPS.
AI.motivation: To resolve the open problem of determining the actual perturbations induced by matrix product state approximations of critical systems, and to address instabilities in automatic differentiation methods for tensor network optimization.
AI.method: Development of a sparse linear solver to compute forward and backward derivatives of 2D tensor networks implicitly, enabling variational optimization of projected entangled pair states while avoiding instabilities of traditional automatic differentiation.
AI.result: Demonstrates that perturbations from MPS approximations of critical systems differ significantly from conformal field theory predictions.
AI.conclusion: Finite entanglement scaling induces perturbations that deviate from CFT expectations, and the proposed sparse linear solver provides a more stable primitive for PEPS variational optimization.

title: Periodic orbits and quantum many-body scars in integrable spin chains
summary: Quantum many-body scars provide an exception to generic thermalising dynamics, but their relation to integrability remains unclear. Here we apply the periodic-orbit framework to the integrable XYZ/XXZ spin-1/2 chain, developing an energy-resolved approach that enables us to locate and track periodic orbits across the spectrum. We identify families of scarred orbits and resolve their supporting eigenstates in terms of Bethe-ansatz quantum numbers, revealing a common string core dressed by zero-momentum magnon pairs. This allows us to reconstruct both the scarred eigenstates and the associated towers directly within the Bethe ansatz, and explain the equidistant tower spacing analytically from the decoupling of zero-momentum magnon pairs in the Bethe equations, providing a microscopic realisation of scar phenomenology in an integrable setting.
